thread.title: Dow Gains 209 Points Because Roller Coasters Go Up, Too

title: Dow Gains 209 Points Because Roller Coasters Go Up, Too
text:
Dow Gains 209 Points Because Roller Coasters Go Up, Too By Nov. 15, 2018 4:52 p.m. ET Order Reprints Michael Haddad Text size
Zig Zag Zoom. Stocks reversed course to end higher on Thursday, as optimism about Apple and U.S.-China trade helped to turn the market’s frown upside down. In today’s After the Bell, we... ...look at tech’s turnaround; ...as well as retail’s retreat; and ...wonder if the Santa Claus rally is as imaginary as Santa himself. All Aboard
Stocks finished Thursday on a high note, with all three indexes rebounding from early losses.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 208.77 points, or 0.8%, to 25,289.27, while the S&P 500 gained 1.1%, to 2730.20. The Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.7%, to 7259.03.
It was a pleasant change from the past month, when markets often saw early gains erased by selling into the close.
Retail was one sector that wasn’t able to pull off a reversal, as investors continue to sell stocks despite strong quarterly results, a pattern that weighed on Walmart (ticker: WMT) today as it hurt Macy’s (M) and Home Depot (HD) earlier this week. Expectations are high given how the sector as rallied, although some out-of-favor names could be poised for a comeback after the holiday shopping season.
At least U.S. retail sales, up 4.3% year over year in October, are still going strong. “Strong economic fundamentals, better inventory management, store optimization, and integration of bricks-and-mortar and e-commerce platforms have all contributed to improvement in the top-line growth for retail,” Moody’s Investors Service’s Mickey Chadha notes, and today’s data continue “the strong trend for 2018 and bodes well for the holiday season.”
By contrast, tech was able to score big gains today, helped by a bullish note on Apple (AAPL) from Morgan Stanley . However, that firm also noted that with tech sector “concentration remains near all-time highs, suggesting it’s probably too early to buy the tech sector broadly.” Investors were less interested in nuance, though, with the Nasdaq easily outperforming the Dow and S&P today.
So we’re all set for a Santa rally, right? Well, not so quickly, says CFRA’s Lindsey Bell . She attributes the market pullback following the start of earnings season to investors adjusting to a new, slower-growth environment, and identified “the trade dispute with China as the single most concerning issue facing the market near term.” While she’s still “cautiously optimistic” that we’ll get a resolution, the stakes are high for the G20 summit at the end of the month, and a “lack of a trade deal or an escalation of the current situation without a plan for resolution by year end could result in an ugly start to 2019 for global equities as well as the U.S.”
That doesn’t sound very promising. But the thing about risk is that, much like science or facts, it exists whether you believe in it or not. UBS’ Dirk Effenberger argues that 2018 has been the year that “markets acknowledged risks.” That means it hasn’t been as easy-breezy as 2017, but “this challenging environment has also had a positive effect on financial markets. The roller coaster of 2018 has shaken investors out of their complacency and brought valuations and volatility back to historical norms across major asset classes.” But a more balanced approach to risk doesn’t mean just a dour outlook, as he believes “that investors, too, need to become increasingly mindful of potential upside scenarios.”
Of course, the thing about roller coasters is that they can be scary and fun at the same time. Few investors would probably say the same about recent volatility, but at least riding out the market’s ups and downs provides longer-term benefits than the rickety thrill of the Coney Island Cyclone .
